items.stem: An indifference curve shows
options: the quantity demanded of a good at each price
combinations of two goods that a consumer can afford with a given income
combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction
combinations of two goods that a firm can produce
items.answer: combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same level of satisfaction
items.markingKey: Every point on one indifference curve gives equal utility; ICs further from the origin give higher utility.

items.stem: Explain why an indifference curve slopes downwards from left to right.
items.answer: If a consumer gains more of one good they must give up some of the other to stay equally satisfied, assuming both goods give positive utility (more is preferred to less).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more of X requires less of Y for same utility; 1 mark: assumption that both goods are desirable [2]

items.stem: Explain why the marginal rate of substitution diminishes as a consumer moves down an indifference curve.
items.answer: As the consumer has more X and less Y, the marginal utility of X falls and the marginal utility of Y rises, so each extra unit of X is worth giving up less Y. MRS = MUx/MUy falls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MUx falls/MUy rises; 1 mark: MRS = MUx/MUy so declines [2]

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve. Units of chocolate bars (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of laptops (Y): 28, 16, 8, 3, 1. Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y when X rises from 3 to 4.
items.markingKey: MRS = −ΔY/ΔX = (8 − 3)/1 = 5 units of Y per unit of X.

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve for a consumer. Units of electric scooters (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of bicycles (Y): 24, 16, 11, 8, 6. (a) Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y between each pair of bundles. (b) Explain what your results show about the shape of the curve.
items.answer: (a) 8, 5, 3, 2 (b) MRS diminishes, so the curve is convex to the origin.
items.markingKey: (a) MRS = −ΔY/ΔX for each move [2]; (b) falling MRS → convex IC, because MUx falls as X rises [2]

items.stem: A low-income household in Esteria spends $180 a week on bread (X, $4 per kg) and other food (Y, $5 per unit). The government subsidises bread so that its price falls to $2 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 45, Y 36; after: X 90, Y 36. (b) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 180/4, M/Py = 180/5; after M/2 [2] (b) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2]

items.stem: Indifference curves are normally convex to the origin because of
options: a diminishing marginal rate of substitution
items.answer: a diminishing marginal rate of substitution
items.markingKey: As a consumer has more X and less Y, they are willing to give up less and less Y for each extra unit of X.

items.stem: Describe the shape of indifference curves for perfect complements, such as left and right shoes, and explain why.
items.answer: L-shaped (right-angled) curves: extra units of one good without the other add no utility, so utility only rises when both are increased together in fixed proportions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: L-shape; 1 mark: fixed proportions, extra of one alone adds no utility [2]

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve. Units of fresh fruit (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of smartphones (Y): 32, 22, 14, 10, 8. Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y when X rises from 4 to 5.
items.markingKey: MRS = −ΔY/ΔX = (10 − 8)/1 = 2 units of Y per unit of X.

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve for a consumer. Units of bus journeys (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of streaming subscriptions (Y): 32, 26, 21, 17, 14. (a) Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y between each pair of bundles. (b) Explain what your results show about the shape of the curve. (c) The price ratio Px/Py is 5. Identify where on this curve a budget line with this slope would be tangent, and explain why that point is the consumer’s equilibrium.
items.answer: (a) 6, 5, 4, 3 (b) MRS diminishes, so the curve is convex to the origin. (c) Between the bundles with X = 2 and X = 3, where MRS = 5 = Px/Py; other points on this curve lie beyond the budget line (unaffordable) and no higher indifference curve can be reached.
items.markingKey: (a) MRS = −ΔY/ΔX for each move [2]; (b) falling MRS → convex IC, because MUx falls as X rises [2]; (c) tangency where MRS = Px/Py identified [1]; reason: highest attainable IC [1]

items.stem: Market researchers in Ostrelia want to understand how consumers choose between printed newspapers and cement. ‘Indifference curves are a useful tool for analysing consumer choice even though they cannot be observed.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: Downward slope from non-satiation; convexity from diminishing MRS; with budget lines they show optimal choice and responses to price and income changes. Arguments against / evaluation: Preferences change and are unobservable; assumes rationality, consistency and transitivity; the theory is a model, judged by its predictions. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: A budget line shows
options: combinations of two goods giving equal satisfaction
the cost of producing two goods
all combinations of two goods a consumer can just afford with a given income and prices
items.answer: all combinations of two goods a consumer can just afford with a given income and prices
items.markingKey: Budget line: Px·X + Py·Y = M.

items.stem: Explain why a consumer cannot choose a point outside their budget line.
items.answer: Points outside require more spending than the consumer’s income at current prices, so they are unattainable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: spending exceeds income; 1 mark: unattainable at given prices [2]

items.stem: Explain the effect on a budget line of a rise in the price of the good on the vertical axis.
items.answer: The Y intercept (M/Py) falls while the X intercept is unchanged, so the line pivots inwards from the X intercept and becomes flatter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Y intercept falls; 1 mark: pivot on X intercept, flatter [2]

items.stem: A consumer has an income of $1200 to spend on streaming subscriptions (X) at $8 each and gym memberships (Y) at $10 each. Calculate the maximum quantity of Y the consumer can buy.
items.answer: 120 units
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/P = 1200/10 = 120.

items.stem: A consumer spends $360 a month on electric scooters (X, $8 each) and gym memberships (Y, $3 each). (a) Calculate the intercepts and the slope of the budget line. (b) Then income rises to $540. Calculate the new intercepts and describe how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) X intercept 45, Y intercept 120, slope −2.67 (b) X intercept 67.5, Y intercept 180; parallel outward shift, slope unchanged at −2.67
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 360/8 = 45; M/Py = 360/3 = 120; slope = −Px/Py = −2.67 [3]; (b) new intercepts and correct description of shift/pivot [2]

items.stem: A low-income household in Lunaria spends $120 a week on maize flour (X, $12 per kg) and other food (Y, $10 per unit). The government subsidises maize flour so that its price falls to $6 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 10, Y 12; after: X 20, Y 12. (b) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 120/12, M/Py = 120/10; after M/6 [2] (b) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between a change in real income caused by a rise in money income and one caused by a fall in the price of one good.
items.answer: A rise in money income shifts the budget line out in parallel (relative prices unchanged). A fall in one price pivots the line, raising real income and also changing relative prices, so it causes a substitution effect as well.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: parallel shift; 1 mark: pivot; 1 mark: relative price change only in the second case [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the effect on a budget line of a rise in the price of the good on the vertical axis. (b) Explain why a consumer cannot choose a point outside their budget line.
items.answer: (a) The Y intercept (M/Py) falls while the X intercept is unchanged, so the line pivots inwards from the X intercept and becomes flatter. (b) Points outside require more spending than the consumer’s income at current prices, so they are unattainable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Y intercept falls; 1 mark: pivot on X intercept, flatter [2] (b) 1 mark: spending exceeds income; 1 mark: unattainable at given prices [2]

items.stem: A consumer has an income of $96 to spend on coffee (X) at $4 each and textbooks (Y) at $2 each. Calculate the maximum quantity of X the consumer can buy.
items.answer: 24 units
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/P = 96/4 = 24.

items.stem: A consumer spends $200 a month on running shoes (X, $4 each) and smartphones (Y, $5 each). (a) Calculate the intercepts and the slope of the budget line. (b) Then the price of X changes to $8. Calculate the new intercepts and describe how the budget line changes. (c) State, with a calculation, whether a bundle of 22 X and 24 Y was affordable before the change.
items.answer: (a) X intercept 50, Y intercept 40, slope −0.8 (b) X intercept 25, Y intercept unchanged at 40; line pivots on the Y intercept, slope −1.6 (c) Cost = 22×4 + 24×5 = $208 > $200, so not affordable.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 200/4 = 50; M/Py = 200/5 = 40; slope = −Px/Py = −0.8 [3]; (b) new intercepts and correct description of shift/pivot [2] (c) cost compared with income [1]

items.stem: A consumer is in equilibrium where
options: the indifference curve meets the X axis
the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve
the budget line cuts the lowest indifference curve
items.answer: the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve
items.markingKey: At the tangency MRS = Px/Py.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain the income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of a normal good.
items.answer: Diagram: X on horizontal axis, Y vertical; original budget line tangent to IC1 at A. Price of X falls, budget line pivots out on Y intercept and is tangent to IC2 at C. A compensating budget line parallel to the new one is drawn tangent to IC1 at B. A→B (movement along IC1) is the substitution effect, an increase in X; B→C (parallel shift) is the income effect, also an increase in X for a normal good.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct pivot; 1 mark: compensated line tangent to original IC; 1 mark: SE = A→B; 1 mark: IE = B→C in same direction [4]

items.stem: Explain why a Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve.
items.answer: A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3]

items.stem: The price of cinema tickets falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 24 units of cinema tickets. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 28 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 33 units. Calculate the substitution effect, the income effect and the total effect, and identify the type of good.
items.answer: Substitution effect = +4 units; income effect = +5 units; total effect = +9 units; normal good.
items.markingKey: SE = B − A = 28 − 24 = +4 [1]; IE = C − B = 33 − 28 = +5 [1]; total = C − A = +9 [1]; classification: IE reinforces SE → normal good [1]

items.stem: The price of bread falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 24 units of bread. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 34 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 39 units. Calculate the substitution effect, the income effect and the total effect, and identify the type of good.
items.answer: Substitution effect = +10 units; income effect = +5 units; total effect = +15 units; normal good.
items.markingKey: SE = B − A = 34 − 24 = +10 [1]; IE = C − B = 39 − 34 = +5 [1]; total = C − A = +15 [1]; classification: IE reinforces SE → normal good [1]

items.stem: The price of fresh fruit falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 20 units of fresh fruit. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 28 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 17 units. Calculate the substitution effect, the income effect and the total effect, and identify the type of good. Explain why this classification matters for the shape of the consumer’s demand curve.
items.answer: Substitution effect = +8 units; income effect = -11 units; total effect = -3 units; Giffen good. The demand curve slopes upwards over this range.
items.markingKey: SE = B − A = 28 − 20 = +8 [1]; IE = C − B = 17 − 28 = -11 [1]; total = C − A = -3 [1]; classification: IE opposes and outweighs SE → Giffen good, Qd falls when price falls [1] Demand curve slope linked to sign of total effect [1].

items.stem: A low-income household in Selmaria spends $360 a week on potatoes (X, $6 per kg) and other food (Y, $3 per unit). The government subsidises potatoes so that its price falls to $3 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 60, Y 120; after: X 120, Y 120. (b) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 360/6, M/Py = 360/3; after M/3 [2] (b) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2]

items.stem: A low-income household in Calvania spends $180 a week on bread (X, $12 per kg) and other food (Y, $5 per unit). The government subsidises bread so that its price falls to $6 per kg. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes. (b) Using indifference curves, explain how the household could buy less bread after the price fall.
items.answer: (a) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper. (b) If bread is a Giffen good, the substitution effect (more bread) is outweighed by a negative income effect: with higher real income the household switches to preferred foods, buying less bread.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2] (b) 1 mark SE direction; 1 mark negative IE; 1 mark IE larger → Giffen [3]

items.stem: For a normal good, when its price falls, the income and substitution effects
items.answer: both increase the quantity demanded
items.markingKey: SE always raises Qd when price falls; for a normal good higher real income also raises Qd.

items.stem: Explain why the substitution effect of a price change always works in the opposite direction to the price change.
items.answer: The substitution effect holds utility constant and considers only the change in relative prices; a fall in price makes the good relatively cheaper, so the consumer moves along the same IC to more of it (convexity of the IC ensures this).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relative price change, utility constant; 1 mark: move along convex IC towards the cheaper good [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the substitution effect of a price change always works in the opposite direction to the price change. (b) Explain why a Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve.
items.answer: (a) The substitution effect holds utility constant and considers only the change in relative prices; a fall in price makes the good relatively cheaper, so the consumer moves along the same IC to more of it (convexity of the IC ensures this). (b) A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: relative price change, utility constant; 1 mark: move along convex IC towards the cheaper good [2] (b) 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3]

items.stem: The price of coffee falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 20 units of coffee. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 28 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 23 units. Which type of good is this for the consumer?
items.answer: inferior
items.markingKey: SE = 28 − 20 = +8; IE = 23 − 28 = -5. IE negative but smaller than SE: inferior (not Giffen).

items.stem: The price of cinema tickets in Dravonia has fallen by 20% over two years. Assess whether a fall in the price of a good will always increase the quantity demanded.
items.answer: Arguments for: For normal and most inferior goods, SE dominates so Qd rises when price falls. Arguments against / evaluation: Giffen goods (strongly inferior staples with a large budget share) and Veblen goods are exceptions; expectations of further price falls; but such cases are rare in practice. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: The price of airline seats in Istrana has fallen by 20% over two years. ‘Indifference curve analysis explains consumer behaviour better than marginal utility theory.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: Ordinal utility only; separates income and substitution effects; explains Giffen and inferior goods; consumer equilibrium at tangency MRS = Px/Py. Arguments against / evaluation: Still assumes rationality, full information and smooth preferences; difficult to observe ICs; behavioural economics challenges both models; both predict downward-sloping demand for most goods. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: The marginal rate of substitution of X for Y measures
options: the amount of Y a consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of X while keeping utility constant
the change in income needed to buy one more unit of X
the extra utility from one more unit of X
the ratio of the price of X to the price of Y
items.answer: the amount of Y a consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of X while keeping utility constant
items.markingKey: MRS = −ΔY/ΔX along an indifference curve; equals the (absolute) slope of the IC.

items.stem: Explain one advantage of indifference curve analysis over marginal utility theory.
items.answer: It requires only ordinal utility: consumers just need to rank bundles, not measure utility in utils. It also separates the income and substitution effects of a price change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ordinal not cardinal; 1 mark: explanation/second advantage [2]

items.stem: Noah is indifferent between 4 units of restaurant meals with 10 units of rice and 6 units of restaurant meals with 7 units of rice. Explain what this tells you about the marginal rate of substitution and the shape of the indifference curve.
items.answer: Noah gives up 3 units of rice for 2 more restaurant meals, so MRS = 1.5 over this range; the curve slopes downwards, and if MRS falls further along it, the curve is convex.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MRS = 3/2 = 1.5; 1 mark: downward slope, convexity from diminishing MRS [2]

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve. Units of textbooks (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of bus journeys (Y): 32, 20, 10, 5, 3. Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y when X rises from 1 to 2.
items.markingKey: MRS = −ΔY/ΔX = (32 − 20)/1 = 12 units of Y per unit of X.

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve for a consumer. Units of streaming subscriptions (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of fresh fruit (Y): 24, 16, 10, 5, 2. (a) Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y between each pair of bundles. (b) Explain what your results show about the shape of the curve.
items.answer: (a) 8, 6, 5, 3 (b) MRS diminishes, so the curve is convex to the origin.
items.markingKey: (a) MRS = −ΔY/ΔX for each move [2]; (b) falling MRS → convex IC, because MUx falls as X rises [2]

items.stem: A low-income household in Halvoria spends $180 a week on maize flour (X, $6 per kg) and other food (Y, $10 per unit). The government subsidises maize flour so that its price falls to $3 per kg. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes. (b) Using indifference curves, explain how the household could buy less maize flour after the price fall.
items.answer: (a) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper. (b) If maize flour is a Giffen good, the substitution effect (more maize flour) is outweighed by a negative income effect: with higher real income the household switches to preferred foods, buying less maize flour.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2] (b) 1 mark SE direction; 1 mark negative IE; 1 mark IE larger → Giffen [3]

items.stem: The slope of a budget line with good X on the horizontal axis is equal to
items.answer: −Px/Py
items.markingKey: Slope = −(price of X)/(price of Y).

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a consumer cannot choose a point outside their budget line. (b) Distinguish between a change in real income caused by a rise in money income and one caused by a fall in the price of one good.
items.answer: (a) Points outside require more spending than the consumer’s income at current prices, so they are unattainable. (b) A rise in money income shifts the budget line out in parallel (relative prices unchanged). A fall in one price pivots the line, raising real income and also changing relative prices, so it causes a substitution effect as well.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: spending exceeds income; 1 mark: unattainable at given prices [2] (b) 1 mark: parallel shift; 1 mark: pivot; 1 mark: relative price change only in the second case [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Distinguish between a change in real income caused by a rise in money income and one caused by a fall in the price of one good. (b) Explain why a consumer cannot choose a point outside their budget line.
items.answer: (a) A rise in money income shifts the budget line out in parallel (relative prices unchanged). A fall in one price pivots the line, raising real income and also changing relative prices, so it causes a substitution effect as well. (b) Points outside require more spending than the consumer’s income at current prices, so they are unattainable.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: parallel shift; 1 mark: pivot; 1 mark: relative price change only in the second case [3] (b) 1 mark: spending exceeds income; 1 mark: unattainable at given prices [2]

items.stem: A consumer has an income of $120 to spend on electric scooters (X) at $5 each and airline seats (Y) at $4 each. Calculate the maximum quantity of X the consumer can buy.
items.answer: 24 units
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/P = 120/5 = 24.

items.stem: A consumer spends $144 a month on airline seats (X, $2 each) and bottled water (Y, $6 each). (a) Calculate the intercepts and the slope of the budget line. (b) Then the price of X changes to $3. Calculate the new intercepts and describe how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) X intercept 72, Y intercept 24, slope −0.33 (b) X intercept 48, Y intercept unchanged at 24; line pivots on the Y intercept, slope −0.5
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 144/2 = 72; M/Py = 144/6 = 24; slope = −Px/Py = −0.33 [3]; (b) new intercepts and correct description of shift/pivot [2]

items.stem: A low-income household in Loristan spends $180 a week on bread (X, $6 per kg) and other food (Y, $5 per unit). The government subsidises bread so that its price falls to $3 per kg. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes. (b) Using indifference curves, explain how the household could buy less bread after the price fall.
items.answer: (a) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper. (b) If bread is a Giffen good, the substitution effect (more bread) is outweighed by a negative income effect: with higher real income the household switches to preferred foods, buying less bread.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2] (b) 1 mark SE direction; 1 mark negative IE; 1 mark IE larger → Giffen [3]

items.stem: A Giffen good is one for which, following a fall in its price,
options: the substitution effect outweighs the income effect
the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so quantity demanded falls
items.answer: the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so quantity demanded falls
items.markingKey: Giffen: strongly inferior good; IE opposite and larger than SE, giving an upward-sloping demand curve.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the substitution effect of a price change always works in the opposite direction to the price change. (b) Explain why a Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve.
items.answer: (a) The substitution effect holds utility constant and considers only the change in relative prices; a fall in price makes the good relatively cheaper, so the consumer moves along the same IC to more of it (convexity of the IC ensures this). (b) A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: relative price change, utility constant; 1 mark: move along convex IC towards the cheaper good [2] (b) 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain the income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of a normal good.
items.answer: (a) A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price. (b) Diagram: X on horizontal axis, Y vertical; original budget line tangent to IC1 at A. Price of X falls, budget line pivots out on Y intercept and is tangent to IC2 at C. A compensating budget line parallel to the new one is drawn tangent to IC1 at B. A→B (movement along IC1) is the substitution effect, an increase in X; B→C (parallel shift) is the income effect, also an increase in X for a normal good.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3] (b) 1 mark: correct pivot; 1 mark: compensated line tangent to original IC; 1 mark: SE = A→B; 1 mark: IE = B→C in same direction [4]

items.stem: A consumer buys restaurant meals (X, $2) and streaming subscriptions (Y, $4). At the current bundle the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y is 1. Explain whether the consumer is in equilibrium and how they should change their purchases.
items.answer: Not in equilibrium: MRS (1) ≠ Px/Py (0.5). The consumer values X more than its relative price, so should buy more restaurant meals and less of the other good until MRS = 0.5.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium requires MRS = Px/Py = 2/4 = 0.5 [1]; MRS > price ratio [1]; buy more restaurant meals; diminishing MRS restores equality [1].

items.stem: The price of bus journeys falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 10 units of bus journeys. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 16 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 8 units. Calculate the substitution effect, the income effect and the total effect, and identify the type of good.
items.answer: Substitution effect = +6 units; income effect = -8 units; total effect = -2 units; Giffen good.
items.markingKey: SE = B − A = 16 − 10 = +6 [1]; IE = C − B = 8 − 16 = -8 [1]; total = C − A = -2 [1]; classification: IE opposes and outweighs SE → Giffen good, Qd falls when price falls [1]

items.stem: A consumer buys concert tickets (X, $5) and smartphones (Y, $6). At the current bundle the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y is 1.5. Explain whether the consumer is in equilibrium and how they should change their purchases.
items.answer: Not in equilibrium: MRS (1.5) ≠ Px/Py (0.83). The consumer values X more than its relative price, so should buy more concert tickets and less of the other good until MRS = 0.83.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium requires MRS = Px/Py = 5/6 = 0.83 [1]; MRS > price ratio [1]; buy more concert tickets; diminishing MRS restores equality [1].

items.stem: A low-income household in Valdoria spends $360 a week on potatoes (X, $6 per kg) and other food (Y, $10 per unit). The government subsidises potatoes so that its price falls to $3 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) With the aid of a diagram, explain how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 60, Y 36; after: X 120, Y 36. (b) The budget line pivots outwards from the Y intercept, becoming flatter; real income rises and X is relatively cheaper.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 360/6, M/Py = 360/10; after M/3 [2] (b) 1 mark pivot on Y intercept; 1 mark flatter/real income rise [2]

items.stem: A low-income household in Tarvia spends $120 a week on potatoes (X, $4 per kg) and other food (Y, $10 per unit). The government subsidises potatoes so that its price falls to $2 per kg. (a) Calculate the intercepts of the budget line before and after the subsidy. (b) Assess whether subsidising a staple food is the best way to raise the living standards of poor households.
items.answer: (a) Before: X 30, Y 12; after: X 60, Y 12. (b) For: raises real income, improves nutrition, simple. Against: benefits richer households too, cost to government, may be inferior/Giffen so consumption may fall; cash transfers allow free choice. Judgement depends on targeting and budget.
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 120/4, M/Py = 120/10; after M/2 [2] (b) 2 marks analysis; 2 marks evaluation [4]

items.stem: Two indifference curves for the same consumer cannot cross because
options: the budget line would then be vertical
this would imply one bundle gives two different levels of utility
items.answer: this would imply one bundle gives two different levels of utility
items.markingKey: Crossing ICs contradict transitivity and “more is preferred to less”.

items.stem: Chloe is indifferent between 4 units of chocolate bars with 10 units of cement and 6 units of chocolate bars with 7 units of cement. Explain what this tells you about the marginal rate of substitution and the shape of the indifference curve.
items.answer: Chloe gives up 3 units of cement for 2 more chocolate bars, so MRS = 1.5 over this range; the curve slopes downwards, and if MRS falls further along it, the curve is convex.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MRS = 3/2 = 1.5; 1 mark: downward slope, convexity from diminishing MRS [2]

items.stem: Tomás is indifferent between 4 units of laptops with 10 units of cement and 6 units of laptops with 7 units of cement. Explain what this tells you about the marginal rate of substitution and the shape of the indifference curve.
items.answer: Tomás gives up 3 units of cement for 2 more laptops, so MRS = 1.5 over this range; the curve slopes downwards, and if MRS falls further along it, the curve is convex.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MRS = 3/2 = 1.5; 1 mark: downward slope, convexity from diminishing MRS [2]

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve. Units of airline seats (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of laptops (Y): 40, 30, 22, 18, 15. Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y when X rises from 1 to 2.
items.markingKey: MRS = −ΔY/ΔX = (40 − 30)/1 = 10 units of Y per unit of X.

items.stem: The bundles below all lie on one indifference curve for a consumer. Units of textbooks (X): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Units of cinema tickets (Y): 28, 18, 12, 7, 3. (a) Calculate the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y between each pair of bundles. (b) Explain what your results show about the shape of the curve.
items.answer: (a) 10, 6, 5, 4 (b) MRS diminishes, so the curve is convex to the origin.
items.markingKey: (a) MRS = −ΔY/ΔX for each move [2]; (b) falling MRS → convex IC, because MUx falls as X rises [2]

items.stem: Market researchers in Dravonia want to understand how consumers choose between electric scooters and bottled water. To what extent do you agree that indifference curves are a useful tool for analysing consumer choice even though they cannot be observed?
items.answer: Arguments for: Downward slope from non-satiation; convexity from diminishing MRS; with budget lines they show optimal choice and responses to price and income changes. Arguments against / evaluation: Preferences change and are unobservable; assumes rationality, consistency and transitivity; the theory is a model, judged by its predictions. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: An increase in a consumer’s income, with prices unchanged, causes the budget line to
options: pivot outwards on the X axis
shift outwards parallel to the original line
pivot inwards on the Y axis
items.answer: shift outwards parallel to the original line
items.markingKey: Both intercepts (M/Px, M/Py) rise in proportion; slope unchanged.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the effect on a budget line of a rise in the price of the good on the vertical axis. (b) Distinguish between a change in real income caused by a rise in money income and one caused by a fall in the price of one good.
items.answer: (a) The Y intercept (M/Py) falls while the X intercept is unchanged, so the line pivots inwards from the X intercept and becomes flatter. (b) A rise in money income shifts the budget line out in parallel (relative prices unchanged). A fall in one price pivots the line, raising real income and also changing relative prices, so it causes a substitution effect as well.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Y intercept falls; 1 mark: pivot on X intercept, flatter [2] (b) 1 mark: parallel shift; 1 mark: pivot; 1 mark: relative price change only in the second case [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the effect on a budget line of a rise in the price of the good on the vertical axis. (b) Distinguish between a change in real income caused by a rise in money income and one caused by a fall in the price of one good.
items.answer: (a) The Y intercept (M/Py) falls while the X intercept is unchanged, so the line pivots inwards from the X intercept and becomes flatter. (b) A rise in money income shifts the budget line out in parallel (relative prices unchanged). A fall in one price pivots the line, raising real income and also changing relative prices, so it causes a substitution effect as well.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Y intercept falls; 1 mark: pivot on X intercept, flatter [2] (b) 1 mark: parallel shift; 1 mark: pivot; 1 mark: relative price change only in the second case [3]

items.stem: A consumer has an income of $96 to spend on cinema tickets (X) at $4 each and textbooks (Y) at $2 each. Calculate the maximum quantity of X the consumer can buy.
items.answer: 24 units
items.markingKey: Intercept = M/P = 96/4 = 24.

items.stem: A consumer spends $180 a month on rice (X, $4 each) and running shoes (Y, $3 each). (a) Calculate the intercepts and the slope of the budget line. (b) Then income rises to $270. Calculate the new intercepts and describe how the budget line changes.
items.answer: (a) X intercept 45, Y intercept 60, slope −1.33 (b) X intercept 67.5, Y intercept 90; parallel outward shift, slope unchanged at −1.33
items.markingKey: (a) M/Px = 180/4 = 45; M/Py = 180/3 = 60; slope = −Px/Py = −1.33 [3]; (b) new intercepts and correct description of shift/pivot [2]

items.stem: In Umbria Nova, money incomes rose by 10% last year while the price of running shoes fell by 10%. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain how a budget line is affected by a change in income and by a change in the price of one good. (b) To what extent do you agree that a rise in income and a fall in price have the same effect on a consumer’s choices?
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Income rise: parallel outward shift, only income effect; price fall: pivot, real income rises plus a substitution effect. (b) Case for the view: Income rise: parallel outward shift, only income effect; price fall: pivot, real income rises plus a substitution effect. Case against / evaluation: Outcomes depend on whether goods are normal or inferior and on preferences; a price fall changes relative prices, so the bundle chosen differs even if utility is the same. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: For an inferior good that is not a Giffen good, a fall in its price
options: raises quantity demanded because the substitution effect outweighs the negative income effect
items.answer: raises quantity demanded because the substitution effect outweighs the negative income effect
items.markingKey: Inferior: IE negative but smaller than SE, so demand still slopes downwards.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain the income and substitution effects of a fall in the price of a normal good. (b) Explain why a Giffen good has an upward-sloping demand curve.
items.answer: (a) Diagram: X on horizontal axis, Y vertical; original budget line tangent to IC1 at A. Price of X falls, budget line pivots out on Y intercept and is tangent to IC2 at C. A compensating budget line parallel to the new one is drawn tangent to IC1 at B. A→B (movement along IC1) is the substitution effect, an increase in X; B→C (parallel shift) is the income effect, also an increase in X for a normal good. (b) A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct pivot; 1 mark: compensated line tangent to original IC; 1 mark: SE = A→B; 1 mark: IE = B→C in same direction [4] (b) 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3]

items.answer: (a) Diagram: X on horizontal axis, Y vertical; original budget line tangent to IC1 at A. Price of X falls, budget line pivots out on Y intercept and is tangent to IC2 at C. A compensating budget line parallel to the new one is drawn tangent to IC1 at B. A→B (movement along IC1) is the substitution effect, an increase in X; B→C (parallel shift) is the income effect, also an increase in X for a normal good. (b) A Giffen good is a strongly inferior good taking a large share of a poor household’s budget. When its price rises, real income falls a lot and the positive income effect (buying more of the cheap staple) outweighs the substitution effect away from it, so quantity demanded rises with price.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct pivot; 1 mark: compensated line tangent to original IC; 1 mark: SE = A→B; 1 mark: IE = B→C in same direction [4] (b) 1 mark: strongly inferior/large budget share; 1 mark: IE opposite to SE; 1 mark: IE larger so Qd and P move together [3]

items.stem: The price of own-brand cereal falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 15 units of own-brand cereal. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 20 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 14 units. Calculate the substitution effect, the income effect and the total effect, and identify the type of good.
items.answer: Substitution effect = +5 units; income effect = -6 units; total effect = -1 units; Giffen good.
items.markingKey: SE = B − A = 20 − 15 = +5 [1]; IE = C − B = 14 − 20 = -6 [1]; total = C − A = -1 [1]; classification: IE opposes and outweighs SE → Giffen good, Qd falls when price falls [1]

items.stem: A consumer buys printed newspapers (X, $4) and smartphones (Y, $2). At the current bundle the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y is 1.5. Explain whether the consumer is in equilibrium and how they should change their purchases.
items.answer: Not in equilibrium: MRS (1.5) ≠ Px/Py (2). The consumer values X less than its relative price, so should buy more smartphones and less of the other good until MRS = 2.
items.markingKey: Equilibrium requires MRS = Px/Py = 4/2 = 2 [1]; MRS < price ratio [1]; buy more smartphones; diminishing MRS restores equality [1].

items.stem: The price of rice falls. In an indifference curve diagram, the consumer’s original equilibrium A involves 12 units of rice. On the compensated budget line (tangent to the original indifference curve) the consumer would buy 18 units (point B). The new equilibrium C involves 21 units. Calculate the substitution effect, the income effect and the total effect, and identify the type of good.
items.answer: Substitution effect = +6 units; income effect = +3 units; total effect = +9 units; normal good.
items.markingKey: SE = B − A = 18 − 12 = +6 [1]; IE = C − B = 21 − 18 = +3 [1]; total = C − A = +9 [1]; classification: IE reinforces SE → normal good [1]

items.stem: Poor households in Gorvania spend about half their income on a staple food. ‘A fall in the price of a good will always increase the quantity demanded.’ Discuss this view.
items.answer: Arguments for: For normal and most inferior goods, SE dominates so Qd rises when price falls. Arguments against / evaluation: Giffen goods (strongly inferior staples with a large budget share) and Veblen goods are exceptions; expectations of further price falls; but such cases are rare in practice. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Poor households in Halvoria spend about half their income on a staple food. To what extent do you agree that indifference curve analysis explains consumer behaviour better than marginal utility theory?
items.answer: Arguments for: Ordinal utility only; separates income and substitution effects; explains Giffen and inferior goods; consumer equilibrium at tangency MRS = Px/Py. Arguments against / evaluation: Still assumes rationality, full information and smooth preferences; difficult to observe ICs; behavioural economics challenges both models; both predict downward-sloping demand for most goods. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.
